It also points out that whoever is able to create man in the state of life he is in, and what follows it of knowledge and action, from a substance that has not even smelled the fragrance of life, let alone other perfections, is able to teach reading to the living, knowing, speaking one. That is, the One who originated creation and singled it out, or who created everything.

The Imam said: You see from the context of the narration we have presented that what is most immediately understood from the meaning of the first verse is: "Be a reader in the name of Allah," in the manner of the existential command (al-amr al-takwini), for the Prophet (ﷺ) was neither a reader nor a writer. For this reason he repeated the statement several times: "I am not one who reads." After that came the divine command that he should become a reader, even though he was not a writer, for a book would be sent down to him which he would read, even though he would not write it. For this reason He described the Lord as "who created," that is, who brought into existence the beings which description cannot encompass, [and who is] able to bring reading into being in you, even though you had not previously learned it, because you did not know what the Book was. It is as if Allah were saying: "Be a reader by My power and My will." He expressed it by the word "name" because, as was mentioned previously in (Surat Sabbih), it indicates that by which the essence is known. The creation of reading draws your attention to the Essence and all its attributes, because reading is knowledge in a living soul. It casts into your mind from Allah His existence, His knowledge, His power and His will.

As for if we take the command as a legal obligation (taklif) and say the meaning is that you are commanded, whenever you read, to read in the name of Allah (and this is contrary to what is most immediately understood), then the meaning would be: whenever you read, read always in such a way that your reading is an act you carry out for Allah and not for anyone else. Even if it were assumed that he read and made his reading for Allah alone and did not mention the Name, he would still be reading in the name of Allah. The verbal invocation of the Name was only requested so that it would alert the heart at the beginning of every act, until it returns to Allah in that act. It is noted that he acts for His Name and not for the name of anyone else, glorified is He. End of quotation. It is good.

﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾: that is, from congealed blood. This is the state of the embryo in the first days of its creation. The specification of the creation of man by mention, among the rest of created beings, is because of his distinctiveness in the wonders of craftsmanship and governance, and to magnify his station, for he is the noblest of them, and to him the revelation is sent down. He is the one commanded to read. He said ﴿clinging substance﴾ and not "a clot" as in the other verse, for the sake of the verse-endings (fawasil), and because "man" is meant in the sense of the species.

So it has the meaning of the plural. For this reason it used the plural for that from which he was created, to match it. It singled out the clinging substance rather than other stages, because it is more indicative of the completeness of power than the lump of flesh, while entailing what preceded it, and for the sake of the verse-endings.

The Imam said: That is: whoever is able to create from congealed blood a human being, who is the living, speaking one who by his knowledge rules over the rest of the earthly creatures and subjects them to his service, is able to make from the complete human being, like the Prophet (ﷺ), a reader, even though he had not previously learned reading. This verse came after the preceding one in order to increase the meaning in emphasis, as if He were saying to the one who repeated the statement that he is not a reader: be certain that you have become a reader by the permission of your Lord who brought the beings into existence, and reading is only one of them. The One who produced man as a complete creation from congealed blood with no form or shape. Reading is only an accidental attribute upon that complete human being, so it is more fitting for easy bringing into existence. And since reading is among the faculties that the soul does not acquire except by repetition and habituation to what is customary among people, the repeated divine command took the place of repeated recitation in making it a faculty for the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason He repeated the command with His words: ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾. The clause "and your Lord" etc. is a resumptive clause explaining that Allah is more generous than anyone from whom giving is hoped, so it is easy for Him to pour this blessing upon you, the blessing of reading, from the ocean of His generosity. Then He wished to increase his assurance with this new gift, so He described the Giver as ﴿who taught by the pen﴾: that is, He made people understand through the pen just as He made them understand through the tongue. The pen is an inanimate instrument with no life in it, and it is not in its nature to convey understanding. So the One who made the dead, silent inanimate object an instrument of understanding and explanation, will He not make you a reader who explains, a reciter who teaches, while you are a complete human being? Then He wished to dispel doubt from himself and remove from him the astonishment at his reading when he had not been a reader, so He said: ﴿taught man that which he did not know﴾: that is, the One whose command was issued that you should be a reader, and who brought into you the faculty of reading and recitation, and will bring you in it to a level no one else has reached, is the One who taught man all the knowledge he enjoys, when at the beginning of his creation he knew nothing. So is it strange that this Teacher, who began knowledge for man when he had no prior knowledge at all, should teach you reading when you possess many other sciences and your soul is prepared by them to receive others? End of quotation.

**Notes:**

**First:** Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Miftah Dar al-Sa'ada*, in the discussions on the wonders of man and what He created in him of wisdom: Then reflect on Allah's blessing upon man with the two forms of expression: the spoken expression and the written expression. He, glorified is He, counted them among the blessings He bestowed upon the servant. In the first surah revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) He said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾ ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿who taught by the pen﴾ ﴿taught man that which he did not know﴾. Reflect on how He gathered in these words all the stages of creation, and how they contain the four stages of existence in the briefest, clearest and finest expression. He mentioned first the generality of creation, which is the giving of external existence, then secondly He mentioned the particularity of the creation of man, because it is the locus of reflection. The verse about it is great, and from witnessing it, there is pure enumeration of blessings. He mentioned here the material of his creation, from the clinging substance. In other places He mentions what precedes it. As for the material of the root, which is dust and clay or the sounding clay like pottery, or the material of the branch, which is the despised water, and here He mentioned the first beginning of the attachment of formation, which is the clinging substance; for before it there was a drop, so its first transition is to the clinging substance. Then thirdly He mentioned teaching by the pen, which is among the greatest of His blessings upon His servants, for by it knowledge is made eternal, rights are established, commandments are known, testimonies are preserved, and the accounts of transactions between people are kept. By it the reports of the past are recorded for those who come after. Were it not for writing, the reports of some periods would be cut off from others, the sunnahs would be obliterated, rulings would be confused, and later generations would not know the doctrines of the earlier ones. Most of the corruption that enters people's religion and worldly affairs comes from forgetfulness, which erases the forms of knowledge from their hearts. So He made the Book a vessel preserving knowledge from loss, like the containers that protect belongings from being lost and destroyed. Thus the blessing of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by teaching the pen after the Qur'an is among the most noble blessings. And teaching by it, although it is something a person reaches through cleverness and ingenuity, the one who attained it and brought him to it is a gift Allah gave him, a favour Allah bestowed upon him, and an increase in his creation and virtue. He is the One who taught him writing. Though he is the learner, his act is an act of response to the teaching of the One who taught by the pen, for He taught him and he learned, just as He taught him speech and he spoke. Moreover, who gave him the mind by which he understands, the tongue by which he expresses, and the fingertip by which he writes, and who prepared his mind to accept this learning in preference to the rest of the animals, and who made his tongue speak and his fingertip move, and who supported the fingertip with the palm, and supported the palm with the forearm? How many signs of Allah we are heedless of in the teaching by the pen. So pause for a moment in the state of writing and reflect on your condition when you hold the pen, which is an inanimate object, and place it upon the paper, which is also inanimate, so that from between the two there come forth kinds of wisdom, varieties of knowledge, arts of correspondence, speeches, poetry and prose, and answers to questions. Who sent the course of meanings upon your heart and imprinted them in your mind, then sent the expressions indicating them upon your tongue, then moved your fingertip with them until they became a wondrous inscription whose meaning is more wondrous than its form, so that by it you accomplish your aims and attain a need in your breast, and send it to distant lands and far regions, where it stands in your place, translates for you, speaks on your tongue, and takes the place of your messenger, and benefits you in ways that a messenger you send would not, except by the One who taught by the pen, who taught man what he did not know? Teaching by the pen entails three levels: the level of mental existence, the level of verbal existence, and the level of written form. So the teaching by the pen has shown that He, glorified is He, is the giver of these levels.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 96, verses 1–5 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying, "Created" (khalaqa), indicates that He bestows actual existence (al-wujud al-ʿayni). These verses, despite their brevity, conciseness and eloquence, indicate that all levels of existence are ascribed to Him, may He be exalted, both in creation and in teaching. He mentioned here among His attributes the name "Al-Akram" (the Most Generous), in which is every good and every perfection. So He possesses every perfection in His attributes, and from Him comes every good in His actions. He is "Al-Akram" in His essence, His attributes and His actions. This creation and teaching arose only from His generosity, His kindness and His benevolence, not from any need that compelled Him to it, for He is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani), the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid).

The second point: The Imam said: There is no more eloquent explanation nor more decisive proof of the virtue of reading (qira'a), writing (kitaba) and knowledge in all its kinds than God's opening of His Book and His beginning of the Revelation with these dazzling verses. If the Muslims do not be guided by this guidance, and the contemplation of it does not awaken them to rise up and tear apart those veils that have shut out the light of knowledge from their eyes, and to break those doors which their leaders have locked upon them, imprisoning them in darkness of ignorance, and if they do not seek guidance from the opening of this clear Book, and do not illuminate themselves with this shining light, then God will never guide them.

The third point: Al-Razi said: In His saying, "Recite in the name of your Lord who created" and "Created man from a clinging substance" (Surah al-ʿAlaq 96:2), there is an indication (ishara) to the rational proof (al-dalala al-ʿaqliyya) that indicates the perfection of power, wisdom, knowledge and mercy. And in His saying, "Who taught by the pen" (Surah al-ʿAlaq 96:4), there is an indication to the written rulings which can only be known through revelation (al-sam'). The first is, as it were, an indication to the knowledge of Lordship (maʿrifat al-ruburiyya), and the second to prophethood (al-nubuwwa). He placed the first before the second as an alert that knowledge of Lordship is independent of prophethood, whereas prophethood is in need of knowledge of Lordship. And His, may He be exalted, saying:

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 96, verses 6–8:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[6–8] ﴿Nay, indeed, man transgresses, ﴾ ﴿because he sees himself self-sufficient.﴾ [al-'Alaq: 7] ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return.﴾ [al-'Alaq: 8]

﴿Nay, indeed, man transgresses, because he sees himself self-sufficient.﴾ [al-'Alaq: 7] That is: truly, man exceeds his limit and acts arrogantly toward his Lord, because he sees himself as self-sufficient. So "kalla" (nay) here carries the sense of "truly" (haqqan), since there is no apparent object toward which a rebuke (radd'") would be directed, owing to the late revelation of this passage relative to what precedes it, as has been transmitted in the reports. Alternatively, it is a rebuke to whoever disbelieves in God's blessing through his transgression, even if it is not mentioned, since the context indicates it. The opening of the surah up to this section points to the great favour of the Exalted upon man. So when "kalla" is said, it is a rebuke to man: his Lord has bestowed upon him the perfecting of his creation and the teaching of what he did not know, and blessings for which there is no equal. Then he disbelieves in his Lord, who did this for him, and transgresses against Him in seeing himself self-sufficient.

Al-Karkhi said: the view of Abu Hayyan is that "kalla" means "alla" (indeed, verily), the introductory particle, and Ibn Hisham endorsed this, with the hamza of "inna" after it being kasra, as after the particle of alerting. In al-Kawashi it is said: "kalla" may be an alerting particle, in which case one pauses on what precedes it, or a rebuke, in which case one pauses on it.

(p-6212) Admonition:

This verse indicates a great principle regarding the praiseworthy acquisition of wealth, which the wise reformers have established, namely that wealth should not exceed the need by much. They said: because the excess of wealth is a destruction of good morals in man, as the noble verse has declared.

Some of the wise said: acquiring wealth for the sake of needs and in proportion to them is praiseworthy under three conditions; otherwise the greed for acquiring wealth is among the most reprehensible of traits. The first condition: that the acquisition of wealth be by a lawful, legitimate means, that is, obtaining it from the gift of nature, or through exchange, or in return for labour.

The second condition: that acquisition of wealth not constrict the needs of others, such as hoarding essentials, or competing with weak craftsmen and labourers, or monopolising what is permissible, such as owning lands which their Creator made a open space for all His creatures. She is their mother: she suckles them with the milk of her springs, feeds them with her fruits, and shelters them in the embrace of her parts.

The third condition for the permissibility of acquiring wealth: that wealth not exceed the need by much, otherwise morals are corrupted. For this reason all the heavenly religious laws have forbidden the consumption of riba (usury), and political, moral and civilisational wisdom has likewise forbidden it. This is for the purpose of preserving equality and closeness among people in financial strength, because riba is gain without material exchange, so it contains an element of injustice; it is gain without labour, so it contains the habit of idleness, which corrupts morals; and it is gain without exposure to natural risks, as in trade, agriculture and property. Moreover, through riba wealth grows, so equality among people is disturbed, as its explanation has already been given at the end of Surah al-Baqarah.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ [al-'Alaq: 8], that is, the place of return is in the Hereafter. Abu al-Su'ud said: it is a threat to the transgressor and a warning to him of the end of transgressors. The shift (in address) is for emphasis in the threat, and "al-ruj'a" is a verbal noun meaning "the returning." The fronting of the adverbial phrase restricts the return to Him, that is: the return of all to the owner of your affair, by death and resurrection, is to Him and not to another, either independently or in partnership, so you will then see the consequence of your transgression. It has also been permitted that the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), with the threat and warning being directed at his condition.

(p-6213) THE INTERPRETATION OF HIS WORDS, EXALTED IS HE:

[9–14] ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 10] ﴿Have you seen if he is upon guidance﴾ [al-'Alaq: 11] ﴿or enjoins righteousness?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 12] ﴿Have you seen if he denies and turns away?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 13] ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 14]

﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 10] That is: he prevents him from prayer. He expressed it with "forbidding" to indicate that he was not capable of anything other than that.

Ibn 'Atiyya (Ibn 'Atiyya) said: The commentators have not differed that the one who forbids is Abu Jahl and the servant who prays is the Prophet (ﷺ), as is related in the two Sahihs. The wording of al-Bukhari is: "From Ibn 'Abbas: Abu Jahl said: 'If I see Muhammad praying at the Ka'bah, I will surely step on his neck.' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'If he had done it, the angels would have seized him.'"

In the verse there is a condemnation and a denunciation of the state of that disbelieber, and an expression of wonder at it, and a declaration that it is so shameful and strange that everyone to whom seeing is possible must see it and be filled with wonder. The word "servant" and its indefiniteness (are used) to magnify him (peace be upon him), and to emphasize the enormity of the forbidding and the intensity of the wonder at it. It has also been said that this is from letting the reins loose in fair speech, since he said "forbids" and did not say "harms," and "a servant" and not "a prophet." The seeing here is visual, and in what follows it is intellectual. Its meaning is: "Inform me." For since seeing was the cause of informing about the seen, the question about it was treated as a question about its object. Thus said Abu al-Su'ud.

(p-6214) The Imam said: The expression "Have you seen" (ara'ayta) has come to be used with the meaning of "Inform me," though in verses such as this one it is not intended as a real request for information, but rather it is intended to deny and denounce what is being asked about. It is as if he says: "How foolish is the mind of this one, whom arrogance drives to forbid a servant of Allah's servants from his prayer, especially while he is performing it."

As for His saying: ﴿Have you seen if he is upon guidance﴾ [al-'Alaq: 11] ﴿or enjoins righteousness?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 12], that is: Have you seen if that forbidder is on a sound path in what he forbids regarding the worship of Allah, or if he is one who enjoins good and righteousness in what he commands regarding the worship of idols, as he believes? The answer to the conditional is omitted, and what follows it indicates it, that is: Does he not know that Allah sees? Accordingly, all the pronouns refer to "the one who forbids." It is also permissible for the hidden pronoun in "was" (kana) to refer to the praying servant, and likewise in "commanded" (amara), so that the meaning is: Have you seen the one who forbids a servant who prays? The one forbidden is upon guidance and commands righteousness. The forbidder denies and turns away. How wondrous is this!

The Imam, may Allah have mercy on him, went in his interpretation of the verse to another meaning, and his expression is: As for His saying, ﴿Have you seen if he is upon guidance﴾ [al-'Alaq: 11] ﴿or enjoins righteousness?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 12], its meaning is: Inform me about his state if that tyrant is upon guidance and on the path of truth, or if he enjoins righteousness in place of forbidding him from prayer; would that not be better and more excellent for him?

As for His saying: ﴿Have you seen if he denies and turns away?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 13], that is: Tell me about his state if he denies what the prophets brought, and "turns away," that is, turns away from good action. Does he not fear that a calamity will strike him, and that there will befall him from the punishment of Allah what he has no power to bear? So the answer to each of the two conditionals is omitted, as you have seen in the explanation of the meaning, and this is commendable brevity, after what indicates the omitted part by His saying: ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 14], that is: Is he ignorant that Allah observes his affair? If he is pious and upon guidance, He will reward him best, and if he denies and turns away, he will not escape His punishment. Then, what the commentators prolong about the second object of the first "Have you seen" and the two objects in the second and third is something without meaning, because the Qur'an is the model of expression, and it used it with one object and with no object at all with the meaning of "Inform me." The clause about whose content one asks takes the place of the objects. The end of his words, may Allah have mercy on him.

**(p. 6215) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[15–19] ﴿Nay! If he does not desist, We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾ ﴿a lying, sinning forelock﴾ [96:16] ﴿Then let him call upon his associates﴾ [96:17] ﴿We will call upon the guards of Hell﴾ [96:18] ﴿Nay! Do not obey him, but prostrate yourself and draw near﴾ [96:19]

﴿Nay!﴾ is a rebuke against the one who forbids prayer. ﴿If he does not desist﴾ means: from this rebellion, from forbidding prayer, and from denying and turning away. ﴿We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾ means: We will certainly take hold of his forelock and drag him by it into the Fire. The *saf'* (سَفْع) is grasping a thing and pulling it forcefully. Seizing by the forelock here is a metaphor for subjugation, humiliation, punishment, and retribution.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a lying, sinning forelock﴾ [96:16], is an apposition (*badal*) to "the forelock." It did not suffice with one of the two phrases because the mention of the first specifies that it is the forelock of the one who forbids, while the second describes it with what indicates the reason for the seizing and its extension to everyone in whom that quality is found. Describing it as lying and sinful, though these qualities belong to its owner, is by way of metonymy (*al-isnad al-majazi*), for emphasis, since it indicates that he is described as lying by a stronger implication, and because, owing to the intensity of his lying, every part of him lies. The same applies to sinning. This is like His saying, ﴿and their tongues describe falsehood﴾ [16:62], and the line of poetry: "Her face describes beauty." It is a figurative usage in which what belongs to the whole is attributed to a part, just as it is attributed to an individual in the saying: "The sons of so-and-so killed a man," while only one of them was the killer.

**A subtle point (*latifah*):**

Al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) said: the nun of "*lanasfa'an*" is written with an alif because it is treated as one pronounced in pause, its being replaced by an alif. Al-Samin said: pausing on this nun with an alif is by analogy with the tanwin, and it is written here as an alif in conformity with the pause, because the rule of orthography is based on the state of pausing and beginning.

﴿Then let him call upon his associates﴾ [96:17] means: the people of his assembly, so that he may prevent those who pray and harm the people of truth who are sincere, relying on his own strength and heedless of the subduing and wrath of the Truth. The clause is either by supposing an elided noun (*mudaf*) or by metonymy, the name of the place being used for those who dwell in it. *Al-nadi* is the assembly in which people gather (*yantadi*), that is, they assemble.

﴿We will call upon the guards of Hell﴾ [96:18] means: the guards of the punishment from His hosts, exalted is He, who will destroy him in this world, or drive him into the Fire in the Hereafter while he is humiliated. "*Sanad'u*" is not written with a waw in the codices, following the orthography that matches pronunciation, or for the sake of harmony with His saying "*fal-yad'u*." It has been said that it is in the jussive (*majzum*) as an answer to the imperative, but this is open to question.

﴿Nay!﴾ [96:19] is a rebuke to the forbidder after a rebuke, and a deterrent following a deterrent. ﴿Do not obey him﴾ [96:19] means: do not obey that transgressor when he forbids you from worshipping your Lord. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, persist in what you are upon of disobeying him, as in His saying, ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ [68:8]. ﴿But prostrate yourself and draw near﴾ [96:19] means: pray to your Lord, draw near to Him through worship, and make yourself beloved to Him through obedience. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating, so increase in supplication."

**Remarks (*tanbihat*):**

First: We have already noted that the verses were revealed concerning Abu Jahl, as is established in the reports. The Imam said: there is no barrier to the verses containing an allusion to him, but they are general in every time and age, as you see. Their address is directed to whoever is addressed, not to the person of the Prophet (ﷺ). And God knows best.

Second: The scholar Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari*: the severity of the threat was directed specifically at Abu Jahl and no similar thing occurred for Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, when he cast the entrails of a slaughtered camel upon the back of the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was praying. This is because although both shared in the general harm during prayer, Abu Jahl added threats, calling upon his followers, and trampling the noble neck. In this there is such exaggeration as warranted hastening the punishment upon him had he done that.
